name: CCAO-F Community Signal
description: 67 supplementary items targeting the topics the unofficial ecosystem stresses. Keyed answers are still grounded in official Anthropic documentation. Deliberately not blueprint-proportional — weighted towards D4 and D6 where the core bank was thinnest.

items.objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks
items.stem: A category manager reuses a prompt for supplier correspondence that opens with the line "You are our procurement lead." A colleague tells her two things: that the role line is what gives Claude procurement knowledge it would not otherwise have, and that a role shorter than a paragraph does nothing at all. Which TWO statements match Anthropic's documented guidance on giving Claude a role? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Setting a role focuses Claude's behaviour and tone for the use case.
A role line supplies subject knowledge Claude would not otherwise hold.
Even a single sentence of role setting makes a difference.
A role has no effect until it runs to a paragraph or more of description.
A role removes the need to give background on the deal in the prompt.
A role makes the figures Claude quotes in that field safe to use unchecked.

items.explanation: Anthropic's prompting best practices give role setting its own short section, and the effect they claim for it is behavioural rather than factual: setting a role focuses Claude's behaviour and tone for your use case, and even a single sentence makes a difference. Nothing in the guidance presents a role as a source of knowledge, as a replacement for background, or as any kind of accuracy guarantee. Context is handled separately: the same guidance devotes a section to adding context and motivation, and tells you to think of Claude as a brilliant but new employee who lacks context on your norms and workflows. The role line and the background are two different jobs.

rationales.B: The documented claim is about behaviour and tone. A role does not add knowledge, and the manager still has to supply the deal facts herself.
rationales.D: The guidance says the opposite in as many words: even a single sentence makes a difference.
rationales.E: Adding context has its own section in the same guidance, and the new employee framing applies whether or not a role has been set.
rationales.F: No part of the prompting guidance ties a role to the accuracy of anything Claude states, so the checking obligation is unchanged.

notes.signal: Unofficial D1 material opens almost every worked prompt with a role line but does not say what Anthropic claims for it, which leaves candidates treating the role as a way of giving Claude expertise. Verified against bank #1: D1-008 keys where instructions live, D1-005 and D1-006 key context and positive specification, and D1-001 keys the golden rule, but no item in bank #1 keys the documented effect of role setting; before this item, role appeared in both banks only inside distractor text.

items.objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks
items.stem: A new user has been told by a colleague that Claude works best on clipped keyword strings and that ordinary sentences waste the model's attention. She has been writing prompts such as "supplier report Q3 summary bullets 200 words" and keeps getting shapeless answers. What does Anthropic's own getting started guidance tell her to do?

options.text: Keep the keyword style and add further keywords until the answer sharpens.
Use a fixed field layout such as TASK, INPUT and LIMIT for every request.
Speak to Claude naturally, as she would to a coworker, and be specific.
Change nothing, because the wording of a request does not affect the answer.

items.explanation: Anthropic's getting started article tells users to speak to Claude like they would a coworker or friend, naturally and conversationally, and its getting started tips are to start with straightforward questions, be specific in requests, and iterate and refine. The keyword habit strips out precisely the words that carry the request: who the report is for, what the summary has to establish, and what would count as a good one. Writing the request as a sentence a colleague could act on is both the documented advice and the same idea as the golden rule of clear prompting.

rationales.A: More keywords do not restore the relationships between them. The documented fix is phrasing the request as a person would phrase it, then being specific about what is wanted.
rationales.B: No fixed field layout of this kind appears in Anthropic's guidance for claude.ai users. Specificity comes from describing the task, not from imposing a template on every request.
rationales.D: Being specific in requests is one of the listed getting started tips, so how the request is worded plainly does affect the answer.

sources.title: Get started with Claude - Claude Help Centre
Prompting best practices - Claude Platform Docs

notes.signal: The keyword-string habit is carried over from search engines and is the first thing new business users do wrong, yet the unofficial guides start at prompt structure and never address how a request should be phrased. Verified against bank #1: D1-001 keys the golden rule and D1-006 keys supplying background as though to someone with no prior knowledge, but neither bank has any item on Anthropic's user-facing advice about the register and phrasing of a request.

items.objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks
items.stem: A communications manager asks Claude for a twelve slide investor update. The deck comes back well organised, but it ignores the corporate slide template she is required to use, and it pads the middle with two summary slides that repeat what earlier slides already said. Which TWO changes match Anthropic's documented guidance for document and deck creation? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Ask for one slide per prompt and assemble the deck herself at the end.
Give Claude the specific template and styles the deck has to follow.
Repeat the phrase no filler three times so the instruction cannot be missed.
Ask for as many features and flourishes as possible so the deck feels fuller.
Tell Claude to match the length to the task and leave out filler sections.
Ask Claude to double-check the finished deck against her brief before replying.

items.explanation: Anthropic documents document creation as something the current models usually get usable on the first try, and the Claude Opus 5 guidance on office and document tasks says to prompt the model with any specific styles or templates it needs to follow. The same page treats deliverable length as a separate lever, because written documents run long by default: it recommends explicit length calibration, telling Claude to match the length of written documents to what the task needs, covering the substance without padding with filler sections, redundant summaries or boilerplate. Those two instructions map onto the two defects she is seeing.

rationales.A: The documentation describes whole decks produced in one pass. Splitting the work into a prompt per slide adds handling and still leaves the template unstated.
rationales.C: Repetition and emphatic wording are not the documented lever here, and heavy wording tends to be followed too literally later. The documented lever is an explicit length calibration.
rationales.D: Asking for as many features as possible is the documented way to get more ambitious output, which is the opposite of the padding problem she is trying to fix.
rationales.F: Claude Opus 5 verifies its own work, and Anthropic advises removing explicit verification instructions because they cause over-verification with no gain in quality.

sources.title: Prompting best practices - Claude Platform Docs
Prompting Claude Opus 5 - Claude Platform Docs

notes.signal: Decks and written documents are the deliverables non-developer candidates produce most often, and the unofficial material covers prompting for text but not for a document that has to satisfy a house template and a length expectation. Verified against bank #1: D1-009 keys the above-and-beyond modifier and D1-019 keys plain-text formatting, but neither bank has an item on prompting for a document or deck, on supplying the template it must follow, or on calibrating the length of a written deliverable.

items.objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests
items.stem: A transformation lead has a genuinely hard, loosely specified piece of work: consolidating three regional processes into one. She has Claude Fable 5 available and cannot decide whether to break the work into small prompts herself or hand the whole thing over. Which approach matches Anthropic's documented guidance for that model?

options.text: Reduce the work to the simplest sub-task she can define and build up from there.
Write the full plan herself and give Claude one step at a time to execute.
Ask for three rival plans up front and choose between them before any work starts.
Give it the whole task and have it scope the work, ask questions, then execute.

items.explanation: Anthropic's guidance for Claude Fable 5 tells you to start at the top of your difficulty range: pick a task harder than you would assign to prior models, and have the model scope it, ask clarifying questions and execute. The same page lists navigating ambiguity among the capability improvements, describing the model as performing well when given complex, multithreaded requests and asked to determine next steps, and it warns that testing the model only on simpler workloads tends to undersell its capability range. Decomposition remains available when she needs to inspect a step, but pre-chopping a hard task is what this guidance argues against.

rationales.A: Anthropic says the reverse for this model: the teams seeing the best outcomes give it their hardest problems, and simpler workloads undersell what it can do.
rationales.B: Feeding one step at a time removes the scoping the guidance asks the model to perform, and it makes her plan rather than the work the limit on quality.
rationales.C: Choosing between plans drawn up before anything has been scoped is not the documented pattern; scoping and clarifying questions come first.

sources.title: Prompting Claude Fable 5 - Claude Platform Docs

notes.signal: Unofficial D1 material teaches decomposition as an unconditional habit, so candidates arrive believing that a harder task always means more chopping. Verified against bank #1: D1-011 keys the two conditions under which explicit chaining is still useful, D1-013 and D1-014 key when to delegate and when to work directly, and D1-015 keys substeps as a documented remedy, but nothing in either bank keys the documented advice to hand a hard, loosely specified task over whole and have the model scope it and ask clarifying questions first.

items.objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality
items.stem: A finance officer pastes a fourteen section policy into Claude Sonnet 5 and asks for it to be rewritten in plain English. The reply rewrites the first section well and leaves the other thirteen untouched. She reports it to her team as a product defect. What does Anthropic's guidance for that model tell her to change?

options.text: State the scope explicitly: every section, not only the first one.
Send the same request again until a reply covers the whole document.
Add that the rewrite is important, so the instruction carries further.
Open fourteen conversations and rewrite one section in each of them.

items.explanation: Anthropic documents Claude Sonnet 5 as interpreting prompts literally and explicitly. It does not silently generalise an instruction from one item to another, and it does not infer requests you did not make. The documented remedy is to state the scope explicitly, and the example given is almost this case: apply this formatting to every section, not just the first one. Read that way the reply is not a defect at all, but a literal reading of an instruction that never said how far it reached.

rationales.B: Resending an unchanged prompt leaves the scope exactly as unstated as it was the first time, so there is nothing for the model to read differently.
rationales.C: Emphasis is not scope. Telling Claude that the task matters says nothing about how many sections the instruction is meant to cover.
rationales.D: Fourteen conversations is a great deal of handling for something one clause fixes, and it splits work the model can do in a single pass.

sources.title: Prompting Claude Sonnet 5 - Claude Platform Docs

notes.signal: Partial completion on a multi-item request is one of the most common things business users report as a bug, and the unofficial guides have nothing on it. Verified against bank #1: D1-016 keys surfacing findings before filtering, D1-023 keys diagnose-then-fix iteration, and D1-024 keys constraining a widened scope, but no item in either bank keys literal instruction reading or the remedy of stating how broadly an instruction applies.

items.objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality
items.stem: A policy officer asks for a full rewrite of a long procedure. The reply stops part way through section four and simply ends. A colleague tells her that Claude has run out of context window and that she should start again with a shorter extract. What does Anthropic's help centre tell her to do?

options.text: Start again with a shorter extract, since the reply cannot exceed what she sent.
Send the previous prompt and the answer so far back and ask Claude to continue.
Move to a plan with a larger context window so replies stop being cut short.
Resend the identical request, because the reply completes on a second attempt.

items.explanation: The help centre article on responses that come back too brief draws a distinction candidates routinely get wrong: Claude's context window applies to the prompts you provide, not to the output it generates. The documented step is to retool the prompt by including the previous prompt and the response so far in the next message, which lets Claude carry on from where it left off. The colleague's diagnosis is the wrong one, and shortening the input is not the remedy the article gives for this symptom.

rationales.A: This treats the input limit as a cap on the answer, which is precisely the distinction the article corrects.
rationales.C: A larger context window governs how much material she can send in, not the point at which a generated answer stops.
rationales.D: Resending the same request is undirected. The documented step is to supply the prior exchange so the answer resumes instead of restarting.

sources.title: Claude's response to my prompt is too brief - Claude Help Centre
My prompt isn't giving me a helpful answer - Claude Help Centre

notes.signal: Context window folklore is the single most confident piece of misinformation in the unofficial material, and an answer that stops mid-sentence is the case where it does most damage. Verified against bank #1 and the other community files: D7-001 covers a message that exceeds the input length limit, D3-022 covers length limits inside long conversations and D3-021 covers degradation as token count grows, but no item anywhere covers an answer that stops part way, and none states the documented distinction that the context window applies to the prompt rather than to the generated output.

items.objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality
items.stem: A strategy analyst has Claude Fable 5 helping her pick a supplier shortlist. The replies keep re-arguing a decision the team settled last week, walk at length through options she has already ruled out, and end without naming a preferred supplier. Which instruction matches Anthropic's documented guidance for this behaviour?

options.text: Ask for the answer twice and keep whichever of the two replies is shorter.
Tell it to act once it has enough information and to give a recommendation.
Tell it not to waffle, not to repeat itself and not to sit on the fence.
Ask it to set out in full why every option was considered before concluding.

items.explanation: Anthropic's guidance for Claude Fable 5 addresses this under longer turns by default, and supplies a sample instruction for keeping the model from overplanning on an ambiguous task: when you have enough information to act, act; do not re-derive facts already established in the conversation or re-litigate a decision the user has already made; and if you are weighing a choice, give a recommendation rather than an exhaustive survey. Every symptom the analyst describes is named in that one instruction.

rationales.A: Picking between two replies by length is a selection rule rather than a change to the prompt, and it does nothing about the settled decision being reopened.
rationales.C: This is a list of things to avoid, and Anthropic's documented steer is to tell Claude what to do instead of what not to do.
rationales.D: Setting out every option in full is the exhaustive survey the guidance tells you to prompt away from, so it would deepen the problem.

sources.title: Prompting Claude Fable 5 - Claude Platform Docs
Prompting best practices - Claude Platform Docs

notes.signal: An indecisive answer that surveys everything and recommends nothing is a common complaint in business use, and the unofficial material treats it as a verbosity problem to be solved with a word limit. Verified against bank #1: D1-021 keys stating a length requirement explicitly, D1-024 keys constraining a widened scope and D1-020 keys removing carried-over verification instructions, but nothing in either bank keys the documented instruction for a model that re-argues settled decisions and surveys options instead of recommending one.

items.objective: Determine when human review or additional verification is required
items.stem: A policy team fact-checks a Claude-drafted consultation briefing claim by claim against the source pack, corrects two figures, and signs the 1,200-word draft off. The head of communications then asks for it at 600 words, so the team gives the approved draft back to Claude and asks for it to be cut by half. The shortened version is due to go to the board this afternoon. What does the earlier fact-check establish about the version that will actually be sent?

options.text: It carries over in full, because a shortening pass can only take material away and has no way of putting a new claim in.
Nothing yet: the shortened text is a fresh output, so its claims have to be checked in the version that will be sent.
It carries over provided the cut is made in the same conversation, since the approved draft is still there in the context.
It carries over once Claude has confirmed that the shortened version preserves every figure that the team checked.

items.explanation: Verification attaches to a particular output, not to a document title. Asking Claude to cut an approved draft is iterative refinement, a documented technique in which Claude's output becomes the input to a follow-up prompt, and what comes back is newly generated text. Compression is where qualifiers get dropped, two findings get merged into one, and a hedged estimate turns into a stated fact, none of which the earlier pass examined. Anthropic's guidance is explicit that hallucination-reduction techniques do not eliminate the problem and that critical information should always be validated, especially for high-stakes decisions, and the support centre warns that Claude can write things that look correct but are very mistaken. The claims in the 600-word version are the ones the board will act on, so those are the claims that have to be checked.

rationales.A: Shortening is generation, not deletion. Claude rewrites the material as it condenses it, which is exactly how a caveat disappears or two separate findings become a single causal sentence that neither source supported.
rationales.C: Having the approved draft in context makes a faithful cut more likely, but it is not a check. Nothing in the conversation compares the new sentences against the source pack, and the team would be relying on the same process that produced the draft.
rationales.D: A confirmation from Claude is a self-report from the process under examination. Anthropic's support guidance is that Claude should not be relied on as a singular source of truth, not that it should be asked to vouch for its own output.

notes.signal: Community study material presents verification as a single gate at the end of a drafting workflow, which leaves candidates with no rule for what a later refinement pass does to a completed check, and cutting an approved draft to length is one of the most common last steps in real office use. Verified against bank #1: D2-006, D2-028 and D2-032 all rebut substitutes for verification, and D2-022 and D2-036 key iterative refinement as a technique, but every bank #1 item checks a single generation once and none addresses re-verification after the text has been regenerated.

items.objective: Apply fact-checking and validation techniques
items.stem: A fundraising manager uploads one 30-page impact report and asks Claude for a two-page donor summary drawn from it. The draft is fluent and reads well, but it contains a sentence attributing a precise 37 per cent improvement to a named 2026 university study, and a sentence dating a partnership announcement to a specific month. Neither the study nor the announcement is anything she recognises from the report. Which check most directly tests those specifics against the material she actually supplied?

options.text: Ask Claude to quote, word for word from the supplied report, the passage behind each figure and named source, and to delete what it cannot quote.
Run the same request several more times and keep the version whose figures and dates recur most consistently across the separate runs.
Ask Claude whether it is confident that the named 2026 study and the 37 per cent figure are accurate, and circulate the draft if it says that it is.
Judge each figure against what she already knows about outcomes in her sector and retain the ones that fall within a plausible range.

items.explanation: Anthropic's guidance on reducing hallucinations lists verifying with citations as a basic strategy: have Claude cite quotes and sources for each claim, and have it verify each claim by finding a supporting quote after generating the response, retracting any claim for which no quote can be found. The related direct-quote technique grounds work in the actual text of a long document. That is precisely the test this situation needs, because the question is not whether the figure is plausible in the abstract but whether the supplied report supports it. Fabricated specifics are dangerous exactly because they are formatted like verifiable ones, so the check has to be against the source rather than against impressions.

rationales.B: Best-of-N verification is documented, and inconsistency across runs is a useful hallucination signal, but the inference only runs one way. A fabrication that reproduces itself consistently passes this test, and the test never touches the supplied report.
rationales.C: Self-reported confidence comes from the same generation process as the claim. Anthropic's support guidance is that Claude should not be relied on as a single source of truth, not that it should be asked to vouch for itself.
rationales.D: A plausibility check is the test a well-formed fabrication is built to survive; 37 per cent looks entirely reasonable, which is why it needs to be traced to a passage rather than weighed against intuition.

notes.signal: Multiple unofficial guides teach candidates to look for invented statistics, invented studies and invented dates as the classic hallucination shape, and one hands-on course builds a lab around checking a draft against an uploaded document. Bank #1 has an item on an invented page reference (D2-001) and a definitional item (D2-002), but nothing that makes the candidate choose the test for a named study and a precise percentage against the supplied source, with best-of-N sitting there as the plausible wrong answer.

items.objective: Evaluate Claude-generated outputs for accuracy and completeness
items.stem: A membership officer uploads twelve regional branch returns and asks Claude for a short summary with the headline numbers. The summary opens by saying that membership across the twelve branches grew by 6 per cent and that total membership now stands at 48,910. She checks every branch figure quoted in the summary against the returns and each one matches. What still has to be checked before the summary goes to the committee?

options.text: Nothing further, because the branch figures have been confirmed at source and the total and the percentage follow arithmetically from figures that are now known to be right.
The summary should be produced twice more from the same returns and the three sets of headline numbers compared, since agreement across runs is what establishes the arithmetic.
Claude should be asked to set out the calculation it performed and to confirm the two headline numbers, since a stated method is what makes a derived figure auditable.
The total and the percentage, recalculated from the twelve returns, because a figure Claude derived can be wrong even when every figure it quoted is right.

items.explanation: Accuracy has to be judged claim by claim, and a total or a percentage is a claim in its own right. The two headline numbers were not read out of any return; they were produced in the same generation pass as the prose around them, so confirming the addends says nothing about the sum. Anthropic's support guidance warns that Claude can write things that might look correct but are very mistaken and that users should not rely on Claude as a singular source of truth. The documented verification move is to trace each claim back to something that supports it and retract what cannot be supported; for a derived figure the support is the calculation over the underlying returns, which the officer has to perform herself. The trap is that a successful check of the quoted inputs feels like a check of the whole summary.

rationales.A: This assumes that arithmetic performed inside a generated response is guaranteed by the correctness of its inputs. The headline numbers are text produced alongside the narrative, not the output of a checked calculation, and either one can be wrong while all twelve branch figures are right.
rationales.B: Best-of-N verification is documented and drift across runs is a genuine hallucination signal, but the inference only runs one way. A miscalculation that reproduces itself passes this test, and none of the three runs is ever compared with the returns.
rationales.C: Displayed reasoning is at best a summary of how an answer was produced and is never an audit trail. A plausible-looking method statement can sit above a wrong number, and asking the same process to confirm its own figure adds no independent evidence.

notes.signal: Community material teaches hallucination-spotting almost entirely as invented facts, invented studies and invented citations, and reduces number-checking to checking figures against the source, which leaves the derived-figure case unaddressed even though it is the everyday one in finance, membership and reporting work. items.objective: Determine when human review or additional verification is required
items.stem: An operations director is setting the threshold at which a Claude-assisted output must be signed off by a suitably qualified person before it leaves her team. She weighs three things for each output: who receives it, how easily it can be corrected or undone, and how consequential the decision it carries is. Which TWO of the following outputs cross that threshold? Select TWO.

options.text: A shortlist of possible venues for the team away-day, shared with the four colleagues who are organising the day between them.
A letter to a customer declining an insurance claim, drafted from the policy wording and posted under the company's name.
A message to an unsuccessful job applicant setting out why the application did not proceed, drafted from the interview record.
A summary of yesterday's stand-up posted to the team's own channel, which everyone who attended can read and correct.
A list of proposed discussion topics for a supplier's quarterly review, emailed in advance to the account manager, who can add to it or amend it.
A plain-English explainer on the new expenses rules, posted on the staff intranet, where any member of staff who spots an error can flag it.

items.explanation: All three of the director's tests point the same way for the claim refusal and the recruitment rejection. Each one communicates a decision about a single identified person outside the team; each reaches someone who has no way to correct it and no sight of what it was drafted from; and neither can meaningfully be undone once sent, because the recipient has already been told the outcome. Both also carry the most consequential class of decision on the list, one financial and contractual, the other affecting a person's employment. Anthropic's guidance is that hallucination-reduction techniques significantly reduce hallucinations but do not eliminate them, and that critical information should always be validated, especially for high-stakes decisions; the support centre adds that users should not rely on Claude as a singular source of truth and should carefully scrutinise high-stakes advice. Those obligations bite hardest where the output is itself the decision the recipient receives. The other four outputs each fail at least two of the tests: their readers are the people best placed to spot an error, and a correction costs one further message.

rationales.A: Internal audience, no consequential decision, and trivially reversible. If a venue is wrong a colleague says so and the list changes.
rationales.D: The readers are the people who were in the meeting, so they are the best error detectors available, and any correction is a single follow-up message.
rationales.E: This is the tempting one, because the reader is outside the organisation. An external audience on its own does not settle the question: no decision is being communicated, the account manager can amend the list, and an updated agenda can be sent at any point before the meeting.
rationales.F: Publication feels weighty, but the audience is internal, the explainer informs rather than decides, and the intranet gives every reader a route to flag an error that can then be corrected for everyone at once.

Claude Certified Associate - Foundations Exam Guide, Version 1.0, Section 6 Domain 2 objectives

notes.signal: Community study material teaches escalation as a short list of always-escalate domains, hiring, legal, medical and financial among them, and treats it as the most learnable part of the syllabus, which produces candidates who match on domain words rather than on what the output does to its reader. Verified against bank #1: D2-043 asks which abstract factors should drive the decision, and D2-037 and D2-038 test risk-based review and domain expertise on a single output each; none of them makes the candidate apply the combined audience, correctability and consequence test across a set of concrete outputs, and none of them includes a case where the audience is external but the threshold is not crossed.

items.objective: Evaluate Claude-generated outputs for accuracy and completeness
items.stem: A grants officer puts five specific questions about a funder's guidance pack to Claude in a single message. The reply is a well-organised page that answers three of them in depth and does not mention the other two at all. She checks every statement in the reply against the guidance pack, and every one of them is correct. What is the correct judgement on this output?

options.text: It passes, because accuracy is the property that matters for a factual task, and the two remaining questions can be picked up separately later on.
It passes, because the two questions Claude left out are almost certainly ones that the funder's guidance pack does not address anywhere in its text.
It fails on completeness, because coverage is judged against the five questions asked, so the two unanswered ones must still be dealt with.
It fails, because a reply that leaves questions out shows the guidance pack exceeded the amount of material the model was able to read.

items.explanation: Accuracy and completeness are separate properties, and the D2 objective names both. Anthropic's guidance on defining success stresses that criteria should be specific and relevant to the purpose of the work, and that most use cases need multidimensional evaluation along several success criteria rather than a single one. Here the purpose was to answer five questions, so coverage against those five is a criterion in its own right and a claim-by-claim accuracy check cannot substitute for it. The trap is that a wholly accurate output feels finished. The remedy is to put the two missing questions back, and, following the documented practice of letting Claude say it does not know, to invite it to state explicitly where the pack does not answer a question rather than passing over it in silence.

rationales.A: This treats accuracy as the whole of quality. An output that answers three of five questions is a partial deliverable however sound its content, and deferring the gap leaves the officer working from a summary she may reasonably believe is complete.
rationales.B: This is an assumption presented as a finding. Nothing in the reply says the pack is silent on those questions, and silence in an output is not evidence of silence in the source.
rationales.D: This invents a cause. Omission has many explanations, and diagnosing a context limit from the symptom alone does not tell the officer whether the two questions have answers in the pack.

items.objective: Organize and curate information and select appropriate output formats (artifacts, inline, structured data)
items.stem: A finance assistant has Claude read a folder of supplier statements and pull out roughly 180 line items, each with a date, a reference and an amount. The figures have one destination: the team's existing quarterly spreadsheet model, which already holds the formulas, the pivot tables and the charts that the finance manager relies on. Given that stated downstream use, which output vehicle should she ask for?

options.text: A written summary of the totals in the chat, on the basis that the spreadsheet model already performs all of the arithmetic that matters.
The 180 rows set out inline in the chat as a markdown table, which she can read through and then copy across into the model by hand.
The rows presented as a shareable artifact, so that colleagues can open it, comment on the figures and suggest corrections in place.
The rows produced as a spreadsheet file that she downloads and pastes straight into the existing model.

items.explanation: Format choice follows the consumer of the output. Here the consumer is an existing spreadsheet model, not a reader, so the right vehicle is the one that arrives as data. Anthropic's help centre documents that Claude can create Excel spreadsheets, Word documents, PowerPoint decks and PDFs, and that users can download those files or save them to Google Drive, which is exactly the handoff this task needs. rationales.A: A prose summary answers a different question. It gives the finance manager numbers to read rather than data the model can compute on, and the 180 underlying line items never reach the spreadsheet.
rationales.B: An inline table is a reasonable vehicle for a handful of rows a person will glance at, but at 180 rows the manual copy step is the whole cost of the task and is where transcription errors enter.
rationales.C: Artifacts are documented for content that is significant and self-contained and that you are likely to edit, iterate on or reuse outside the conversation. Collaborative comment and review is not the stated downstream use, and an artifact still leaves the data to be moved into the model.

items.objective: Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses
items.stem: A grants officer asks Claude to draft a funding case using only three documents she has uploaded: a project plan, a monitoring report and a budget. Web search is off. She now reads the draft looking for statements that did not come from those three documents. Which TWO features of the draft are evidence that it has gone beyond the uploaded material? Select TWO.

options.text: A sentence that reproduces a finding from the monitoring report accurately but rounds its figure from 62.4 per cent to a flat 62 per cent.
A widely reported sector statistic that is entirely correct and that none of the three uploaded documents contains.
A paragraph that draws together a point from the project plan and a related point from the budget into a single argument.
A passage that restates the project's main objective twice, once in the opening section and again in the closing section of the case.
A named evaluation study, cited with its year in support of the project's method, that appears nowhere in the three documents.
A sentence reporting the contingency line from the budget and marking it as an estimate rather than as a committed figure.

items.explanation: For a deliverable that is supposed to rest on supplied documents, the test is whether the uploads contain the claim, not whether the claim happens to be true. Anthropic documents external knowledge restriction, explicitly instructing Claude to use only information from provided documents and not its general knowledge, and verify with citations, having Claude find a supporting quote for each claim after generating a response and retract any claim it cannot support. Both keyed features fail that test: neither the sector statistic nor the named study can be traced to the plan, the monitoring report or the budget. The correct statistic is the more dangerous of the two, because a reviewer who knows the sector will recognise it and wave it through, and it will still be unsupported when the funder asks where it came from. The remaining features are either faithful to the uploads or observations about how the draft is written.

rationales.A: The figure is in the monitoring report and the sentence can be traced to it. Rounding is a fidelity point to correct in editing, and a fairly minor one, but it is not a claim that came from outside the pack.
rationales.C: Drawing supplied points together into an argument is the work that was asked for. Both halves trace back to an upload, and synthesis of provided material is not the same as importing material.
rationales.D: Repetition across sections is a structural or editorial defect. It affects how the case reads and says nothing at all about where the content came from.
rationales.F: This reports a line that is in the budget and labels it honestly as an estimate. Marking a figure as provisional makes a claim easier to check rather than harder, and the claim is grounded in the uploads either way.

items.objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
items.stem: A shared services team is deciding between two Claude models for a document review workload. To keep the trial manageable they assemble a sample of the most typical, everyday documents, run both models over it, find the results almost indistinguishable, and prepare to standardise on the cheaper of the two. Against Anthropic's published guidance on optimising for cost and intelligence, what is wrong with that comparison?

options.text: The sample is the wrong slice of the workload: models should be compared on the hardest tenth of the tasks rather than the typical one.
The sample is too small: a comparison between two models is not considered valid until several hundred documents have been put through each of them.
The wrong figure is being compared: the decision should rest on the published per-token price of each model, which is what determines the monthly bill.
The sample is fine, but both models should have been run at the maximum effort setting, so that each one was judged at the top of its range.

items.explanation: Anthropic's cost and intelligence guidance says to price the tail of the workload rather than the median, and to compare models on the hardest tenth of the tasks rather than the typical one. The reason given is that on a typical task every model looks similar and the cheapest looks best, but the bill is decided by the tasks the cheaper model fails: a failed task still bills its tokens, then the retry, then whatever the failure costs downstream. The same page notes that the tail dominates spend even when nothing fails, citing a 20-problem run in which two problems carried 43 percent of the cost. A trial built only from everyday documents is therefore structurally incapable of showing the difference that will decide the bill.

rationales.B: No minimum sample size is published. The documented instruction concerns which slice of the workload the sample is drawn from, not how many items it contains.
rationales.C: Per-token price is the wrong unit. For anyone choosing or switching models the documented rule is to compare on cost per completed task rather than per token, because a more capable model can finish a task with fewer turns and less rework.
rationales.D: Pinning both models at maximum effort is not the documented method. Below a model's ceiling the highest effort levels pay for depth the task never uses, so the guidance is to sweep two or three effort levels on a sample of real traffic rather than to fix effort at the top.

Haiku, Sonnet and Opus differ mainly in response speed, and their accuracy on hard reasoning is much the same
Sonnet is the slowest and costliest of the three and is held back for the hardest reasoning work
Of Haiku, Sonnet and Opus, Haiku is the fastest and lowest cost and Opus is the strongest of the three

items.explanation: Anthropic's Models overview presents the current line-up in a comparison table whose columns run Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 5, Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Haiku 4.5. Compare the two on accuracy, quality and edge cases, then weigh performance against cost
Settle the per-token price difference first, and run the quality comparison only if the two prices turn out to be close
Force the highest effort setting on both tiers so the comparison is made at each model's ceiling

Training data cutoff is the date up to which the model's answers can be trusted, and reliable knowledge cutoff is the date on which that model was released to the public.
The two are the same measurement published twice for different audiences, one figure for claude.ai users and one for developers, so either of them may be quoted.
Reliable knowledge cutoff describes the model when web search is switched on, and training data cutoff describes it when it is answering with no tools at all.

items.explanation: The Models overview publishes both fields for every current model and defines them: reliable knowledge cutoff indicates the date through which a model's knowledge is most extensive and reliable, while training data cutoff is the broader date range of training data used. The two can differ, and in the current line-up they differ for Claude Haiku 4.5, listed at a reliable knowledge cutoff of Feb 2025 against a training data cutoff of Jul 2025. Haiku 4.5 also carries the oldest reliable cutoff of the current four, where Claude Opus 5 carries the newest at May 2026, so the tier a team picks also decides how recent its unaided knowledge is.

rationales.B: This swaps the two definitions and invents a third meaning. Neither field is a release date; the reliable knowledge cutoff, not the training data cutoff, is the one that marks where knowledge is most extensive and reliable.

She plans to add both through the Google Drive integration. Which requirement does the scope have to account for?

Both file types are supported, so the only thing left to check is that the two documents together fit the context window.

items.stem: A team is integrating Claude into a Slack channel used by ten colleagues. The team lead assumes that when Claude works in that channel it reaches each connected system with the permissions of whoever tagged it, so a junior member's request will see less than her own. How should that assumption be corrected?

In a channel Claude combines the connectors on every member's own Claude account, so its reach grows as people join.
In a channel Claude acts with its own service accounts, so everyone there gets the same capability whoever asked.
In a channel Claude acts as the person who created the channel, so its reach follows whatever that colleague can open.

items.explanation: In Slack channels Claude acts with its own service accounts rather than as a specific user, and what it can reach in a channel comes from the access bundles an admin attached to that channel's scope. Anthropic states the consequence directly: anyone in the channel gets the same capability, and what Claude can do never changes based on who asked. A shared channel uses only the service-account connections an admin attached, not connectors on anyone's own Claude account. Direct messages are the opposite case, because there is no scope to attach an identity to, so a DM session runs on the individual's own account with their personal connectors.

options.text: It keeps running if its creator leaves the organisation, but stops firing if the creator is removed from the channel.
It runs with its creator's personal connectors, so it fails the moment that colleague's own access is withdrawn.
It is visible only to its creator, so the team must recreate it before anyone else can see what it is scheduled to do.
Any member of the channel can list, edit or disable it, so it does not have to be handed over with the person.
It has to be recreated whenever it changes owner, because a job stays bound to the account that first scheduled it.

items.explanation: Standing work belongs to the channel it was set up in. Anthropic documents that a job runs with the channel's connections, the same as an interactive request; that standing work is visible to the channel, because jobs post into the channel they belong to; and that anyone in the channel can list, edit or disable it. On continuity the rule is specific: routines keep running if their creator leaves the organisation, but stop firing if the creator is removed from the channel. Integrating an automated step therefore means watching channel membership, not account status.

rationales.B: A job runs with the channel's connections, the same as an interactive request. Personal connectors apply in a direct message, where there is no channel to scope the session to.
rationales.C: Standing work is visible to the channel, because jobs post into the channel they belong to, and any member can ask Claude to list that channel's routines.

items.objective: Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration
items.stem: A marketing lead has written into her team's standing instructions, 'Never send anything to the customer mailing list without my approval.' She tells her director that this makes an unapproved send impossible. How should that claim be corrected?

options.text: The instruction applies only to threads she starts herself, so it belongs in the team's shared memory rather than instructions.
The instruction will hold reliably, but only if it is restated at the beginning of every individual task she assigns.
Instructions steer Claude but do not restrict it, so a decision that must come back to a person needs an enforced control too.
The instruction is unnecessary, because Claude is unable to take any action that reaches people outside the organisation.

items.explanation: Anthropic documents this explicitly: constraints written into a task, and standing instructions of this kind, steer Claude but do not restrict Claude from performing a specific action or from deciding on its own, because anything typed to Claude goes into its working context, where it can be forgotten or overridden. Actions Claude must not take have to be enforced outside the conversation, through permissions and required approval checks in the system where the action actually happens. For a mailing list that means a send permission or an approval gate in the mailing tool, not a sentence in the instructions.

rationales.A: Standing instructions apply to every new session in that scope, not only to threads the author starts, and moving the rule to memory would make it weaker rather than stronger.
rationales.B: Repetition raises the odds that Claude follows the instruction but does not change its nature. Steering is still not a restriction, however often it is stated.
rationales.D: Claude can act through connected tools, which is precisely why external-facing actions need an enforced gate in the source system.

A requirement that the work be split across several channels, so that each part of the deck is produced in a separate place.
A requirement that the team ask for a progress update whenever they want one, so that nothing has to be posted before the end.

items.stem: A compliance team is running a review in which every reviewer must work from the exact version of the supplier policy that was approved in March. That document is still being edited in Google Drive ahead of the next release. A colleague suggests adding it through the Drive integration so nobody has to hunt for it. What is wrong with that suggestion, and what should the team do?

options.text: The integration cannot read policy documents at all, so the team should paste the policy text into the conversation instead.
The integration would expose the March version to the whole organisation, so the team should tighten the sharing settings first.
The integration adds documents to chats but never to projects, so the team should upload the policy to a project instead.
The linked document keeps syncing with later edits, so the team should attach a fixed copy of the March version.

items.explanation: The same live-sync behaviour that makes a connector right for volatile data makes it wrong here. Anthropic documents that a document added through the Drive integration continues syncing with the latest version, so reviewers would silently start reading the in-progress draft rather than the approved March text. When the workflow depends on a specific point-in-time version, the static copy is the correct choice.

rationales.A: The integration reads Google Docs, including policy documents, up to the documented size limit. The problem is version drift, not capability.
rationales.B: Access follows the user's existing Drive permissions - only documents the user can already view can be synced - so adding it does not widen who can see the file.
rationales.C: The integration works in chats and in private projects, so the statement misdescribes the product. It is shared projects the integration does not cover, and in any case moving the document would not address the version drift that is the actual problem.

The weekly active member count shown on the organisation's usage analytics dashboard for the pilot period.
The total number of conversations the team started in Claude across the six months of the pilot.
The proportion of Claude's drafted responses that reviewers accepted without correction, tracked across the pilot.
The estimated time saved figure from the analytics dashboard, presented on its own as the headline result.

items.explanation: Anthropic's guidance on defining success criteria is that a good criterion is specific, measurable, achievable and relevant, and the documented worked example states its target as an improvement over the current baseline. Quality needs a measure of its own, and the share of drafted responses accepted without correction is one the team can track through the pilot. Together they speak to time and to quality, which is what the budget holder is asking about.

items.objective: Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders
items.stem: A sceptical director says, 'If I cannot rely on it being right every single time, it is no use to us.' The team's workflow has Claude check supplier documents against a data-handling policy and post one finding per checklist item. What is the strongest response to the director?

options.text: Point out that the workflow has not yet produced an incorrect finding, so the concern is theoretical rather than practical.
Offer to add a second Claude session that checks the first session's findings before any person reads them.
Explain that each finding names the section it came from, so reviewers can check findings in proportion to the stakes.
Agree to restrict the workflow to documents where an incorrect finding would carry no consequence whatsoever.

items.explanation: Anthropic's documented pattern for this workflow is to ask for the section each finding was based on, because that keeps every finding checkable - the reviewer can open what Claude read. The accompanying guidance is to read the findings before acting on them, in proportion to what is at stake. The honest answer to the director is therefore not a claim of perfect reliability but a design in which the output is verifiable and human review is proportionate to risk.

rationales.A: An absence of observed errors is a weak argument, and it concedes the director's framing that value depends on never being wrong.
rationales.B: Stacking a second automated pass adds cost without adding independent verification, and it removes the human reviewer the guidance places in the loop.
rationales.D: Confining the workflow to consequence-free documents surrenders the value case, when the documented answer is proportionate review rather than avoidance.

items.objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization
items.stem: A team's daily automated digest is accurate but nobody reads it. Every post is a different length, the items appear in a different order each day, and routine items are mixed in with the ones that need somebody to act. What does Anthropic's guidance say to change?

options.text: Run the digest less often, so that each post carries more material and the channel receives fewer of them overall.
Spell out the shape of each post in the job: how long each item runs, the status legend to use, and what to leave out.
Move the digest into a direct message with each reader, so that everyone receives the summary that matches their interests.
Ask Claude to rank the items by importance each day and let it choose the length and layout that suit that day's contents.

items.explanation: The documented instruction is to specify the output format for anything recurring. A monitor or digest that posts on a schedule posts to the channel repeatedly, so spell out the shape you want each post to take: say how long each item should be, give it the status legend to use, and tell it what to leave out, so the channel can read every post at a glance. The routines guidance repeats the point, to name the output format in the job so recurring posts stay scannable, and the project-digest recipe says to name the format in the prompt so every digest comes back in the same readable shape. Once a post matches the format you want, you can also point at it and ask for that format going forward.

rationales.A: Frequency is not what makes the posts unreadable. A less frequent digest in an unpredictable shape is still unpredictable, and it delays anything that needs someone to act.
rationales.C: A digest sent to individuals leaves the channel without the standing record, and it multiplies the work instead of fixing the format. Standing work posts into the channel it belongs to.
rationales.D: Letting Claude choose the layout each day is the cause of the problem. The point of specifying the format is that every post can be read at a glance because every post has the same shape.

The conversation shares normally as soon as her colleague has authenticated the same connector, because sharing is checked against the recipient.
A chat that includes synced connector content cannot be shared, so her colleague should ask the question himself once he has connected the service.
Sharing is blocked because the spreadsheet is above the file size allowed in a shared conversation, so a smaller extract would share normally.

items.explanation: Anthropic lists three connector conditions for Team and Enterprise plans: access permissions are enforced at the user level and each person authenticates with the third-party service when first using the connector, connectors are only available in private projects, and chats with synced content cannot be shared. The restriction attaches to the conversation itself rather than to the recipient, so there is no setting to unlock it. items.stem: A company reissued its expenses policy in June, raising the threshold above which a receipt is required. items.stem: An analyst has spent an afternoon in an ordinary standalone chat working out how to present a new reporting metric. The work belongs with her monthly reporting project, and she wants that conversation filed there rather than left loose in her chat list. She does not want to redo any of it. What should she do?

options.text: Export the conversation and upload the transcript into the project's knowledge, because a chat can join a project only as a knowledge file.
Copy the project's instructions into the standalone chat, because a conversation started outside a project can never afterwards be brought into one.
Add the existing chat to the project from the dropdown beside the chat name, which files the conversation inside the project.
Open a new chat inside the project and paste the whole transcript into her first message, as that is the only way to carry the work across.

items.explanation: Anthropic documents that a standalone chat can be moved into a project using the dropdown arrow next to the chat name and the Add to project option. A project is a self-contained workspace with its own chat history and knowledge base, so filing the conversation there keeps it with the rest of that work. Nothing has to be exported, retyped or rebuilt.

rationales.A: Uploading a transcript converts a conversation into reference material and still leaves the original chat outside the project; the chat itself can simply be moved.
rationales.B: A standalone chat is not permanently stuck outside a project, and hand-copying instructions duplicates configuration the project already holds.
rationales.D: Recreating the conversation by hand duplicates the work, and a transcript pasted into a message is not the same as the chat being filed in the project.

items.stem: A marketing manager on a Team plan makes her campaign project visible to the whole organization. Its knowledge includes a client's unreleased pricing document, and she has already held several conversations inside the project. Which TWO consequences should she expect? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Everyone in the organization can view and use the project, the client pricing document in its knowledge included.
The conversations she has already held inside the project become visible to the organization along with the project itself.
Organization-wide visibility extends to the instructions only, and the knowledge files stay restricted to members she has invited by name.
Her existing conversations inside the project remain private to her unless she chooses to share them individually.
Making a project organization-wide promotes every member to Can edit, so any of them is then able to replace its knowledge.
An administrator is able to allow organization-wide visibility only for those projects that hold no uploaded knowledge files.

items.explanation: Anthropic documents that with a public project everyone in your organization can view and use the project, and that members with view access can see the project contents, knowledge and instructions. It separately documents that your chats within a project are private and inaccessible to other members of your organization unless you manually share them. So the unreleased pricing document becomes readable organization-wide, which is the risk she needs to weigh, while her own conversations do not.

rationales.B: Conversations held inside a project are private by default; sharing the project does not share the chats within it.
rationales.C: Members with view access see the project's contents and knowledge as well as its instructions, so the knowledge files are not held back.
rationales.E: Visibility and permission level are separate settings. Making a project public does not confer Can edit; that permission is granted deliberately.
rationales.F: Administrators can disable public projects for the organization altogether, but that control is not conditioned on whether a project has files attached.

items.stem: A category manager receives a supplier quote marked commercial in confidence and wants Claude to compare it against two earlier quotes. She has a personal Claude Pro subscription, and her employer has a Claude Enterprise plan on which she is already provisioned. Company policy permits supplier pricing in the approved workspace. What should she do?

options.text: Use the personal Pro account, having first switched the model improvement setting off in privacy settings.
Use the employer's Enterprise workspace, the account covered by the company's commercial agreement.
Use the personal Pro account in an Incognito chat, so that the exchange is not retained.
Use either account, because the same underlying models and safeguards apply to both.

items.explanation: Confidential business material belongs in the account that the employer's commercial agreement covers. On Claude for Work plans the organisation manages the account and all associated data, Anthropic acts as a processor under that agreement, and inputs and outputs from commercial products are not used to train models by default. A personal consumer subscription sits outside all of that, whatever the individual settings say.

rationales.A: The model improvement control changes one consumer setting; it does not place the conversation under the employer's commercial agreement, give the employer retention control, or provide admin visibility.
rationales.C: Incognito affects whether the chat is used to improve Claude and whether it is kept in history. It does not make a personal account an appropriate home for confidential company material.
rationales.D: The models may be the same, but the contractual position, retention controls and organisational governance are not. The account matters, not the model.

items.objective: Apply data sensitivity, regulatory, and privacy considerations
items.stem: A recruitment coordinator wants Claude to check a candidate CV against the essential technical criteria in a job specification. Her employer permits CVs in the approved Claude workspace but requires that only the data the task needs is included. Which redaction leaves the task workable?

options.text: Remove the employment dates and job titles, and keep the name and contact details so the file stays identifiable.
Replace every proper noun, including former employer names and the names of technology products, with placeholders.
Remove the name, contact details, address and photograph, and keep the skills, qualifications and history.
Leave the CV intact and add an instruction telling Claude not to retain or reuse the personal details it contains.

items.explanation: Redaction is a matter of stripping what identifies the person while keeping what the task is actually judged on. The essential criteria are assessed against skills, qualifications and experience, so those stay; name, contact details, address and photograph carry no analytic value here and are the direct identifiers. Anthropic's Privacy Policy makes the submitter responsible for having the rights to include personal data in inputs, and notes that personal data in inputs may be reproduced in outputs, which is a further reason to leave it out.

rationales.A: This is backwards. It strips the evidence the criteria are assessed against and keeps precisely the identifiers that should have gone.
rationales.B: Over-redaction. Removing former employer names and technology product names destroys the relevant experience signal, so the check cannot be performed.
rationales.D: An instruction in the prompt is not a technical control. The data is still submitted, and the obligation to minimise what is submitted is not discharged by asking the model to disregard it.

Anthropic's Usage Policy is the governing document for the product, so she may proceed as planned.
She may proceed if she anonymises the list, because anonymisation removes the need for the approval.
She should ask Anthropic to confirm in writing that the intended use is permitted under its policy.

She would like Claude's help summarising the obligations it places on her team. Applying the principle that uncertain material should be treated as sensitive, what should she do?

options.text: Upload it and ask Claude to assess whether the content looks confidential before she relies on the summary.
Upload it in a chat she deletes immediately afterwards, which limits how long the exposure lasts.
Upload it with the partner organisation's name removed, which is enough to de-identify a commercial document.
Treat it as confidential and confirm its status with the partner or the contract owner before uploading.

items.explanation: The default exists because the classification decision cannot be made after the fact. Anthropic's Privacy Policy places responsibility on the person providing inputs for having the necessary rights, permissions or authority to do so, which is a judgement to be settled before submission. When the status of a document is unknown, the conservative handling applies until someone with authority confirms otherwise.

rationales.B: Deletion shortens retention but does not undo the submission, and it does nothing about whether she had the right to submit the partner's document at all.
rationales.C: A commercial contract is identifiable from its terms, parties, dates and figures. Removing one name does not de-identify it, and confidentiality here is about the content, not the label.

options.text: The personal account sits outside the firm's commercial agreement, so the firm has no processing terms, retention control or admin visibility.
Switching the model improvement setting off on the personal account makes it contractually equivalent to working in the firm's Enterprise workspace.
Any zero data retention agreement the firm holds with Anthropic follows the person rather than the plan, so it reaches his personal account too.
Free, Pro and Max are documented as plans for individual users, with Team and Enterprise as the business offerings for work of this kind.
Anthropic notifies the organisation's administrators whenever an employee signs in to a personal account and uses it for the firm's material.

items.explanation: Shadow AI is a contractual and governance problem before it is a technical one. Claude for Work data is governed by the agreement between Anthropic and the organisation, with the organisation's Primary Owner managing the account and its data; none of that reaches a personal subscription. Separately, Anthropic documents Free, Pro and Max as plans intended for individual users and points businesses and teams to the Team and Enterprise plans, so client deliverables on a personal Pro account are in the wrong place whoever is paying for it.

rationales.B: The setting governs whether conversations are used to improve Claude. It creates no data processing terms, no organisational retention control and no admin visibility, which are the things the Enterprise plan supplies.
rationales.C: Zero data retention is approval-gated and applies to eligible commercial surfaces. It has never covered consumer plans, and cannot be extended to one by the employee's intent.
rationales.E: There is no such notification. Discovering unmanaged accounts is something the organisation has to do for itself, for example through domain claiming on Enterprise plans.

items.stem: An Enterprise administrator discovers around forty personal Claude accounts registered on the company's verified email domain, several of them holding client work. She wants those accounts and the content already in them brought into the company's Enterprise workspace, not merely blocked. Which capability does that?

options.text: Tenant Restrictions, which relocate existing personal accounts into the organisation's Enterprise workspace.
Organization instructions, which direct Claude to decline work submitted from personal accounts.
Custom data retention controls, which apply the organisation's retention period to those accounts.
Domain claiming, which surfaces personal accounts on a verified domain and gives users a migration window.

rationales.C: Custom data retention controls set retention inside the Enterprise organisation. They do not apply to accounts that are not part of it.

items.stem: A wellbeing lead has noticed that Claude sometimes shows a crisis support banner when a conversation touches on distress, and wants to write it into the staff wellbeing policy as an escalation route: if someone is struggling while using Claude, the system will notice and the organisation will hear about it. What is the accurate position?

options.text: Enterprise administrators are notified whenever a banner is shown to a member of their organisation, which is what would make an escalation route of it.
The banner is written by Claude as part of its own response, so both its wording and the threshold at which it appears can be set organisation-wide.
The banner offers the user independent helpline services; the responders are not Anthropic staff, and nothing reaches the employer.
The banner cannot be dismissed until the user has made contact with one of the listed services, which is precisely why it can be relied on here.

items.explanation: The crisis banners are produced by a detection system that sits separately from Claude, and what they offer the user is a route to independent crisis helplines. Anthropic's documentation is explicit that helpline responders are not Anthropic employees and that the user's Claude activity stays private, that contact can be anonymous, and that a user may dismiss a banner with no consequence for their account, after which it does not reappear for around two hours. It is a signpost offered to an individual, not a monitoring or reporting channel. An employer that writes it into a policy as an escalation route has both misdescribed a safety feature and left the duty of care it was meant to discharge with nothing behind it.

rationales.A: There is no such notification, and building one would defeat the point of the feature. Nothing about a banner is reported to an administrator or an employer.
rationales.B: A separate detection system, not Claude, decides when the banner appears. It is not part of the model's response and is not something an organisation configures.
rationales.D: Users can dismiss the banner, and doing so carries no consequence for the account. A prompt the user is free to close is not a control an employer can lean on.

items.objective: Follow organizational AI policies and governance standards
items.stem: An operations manager has kept several thousand Claude outputs from a document categorisation workflow. Two reuse proposals reach her for sign-off: building a narrow in-house tool that sorts documents into the same categories, and building a general purpose in-house chatbot that staff can ask anything. Under Anthropic's terms on reusing outputs, what should she tell them?

options.text: Both proposals are fine, because the customer owns the outputs Claude produces and may put them to whatever purpose it chooses.
The categorisation tool is permitted; the general purpose chatbot is not, absent written permission from Anthropic.
Neither is permitted, because outputs may only be used inside the workflow and the product that produced them.
Both are permitted so long as a person reviews the outputs first and the resulting tool is kept inside the company rather than sold on.

items.explanation: Anthropic's guidance on reusing outputs draws the line at competing models rather than at reuse in general. The customer owns the outputs and may build specialised tools from them, with content categorisation, sentiment analysis, summarisation and information extraction given as examples, and may integrate them into its own applications. What is off limits without written permission is using outputs to train general purpose chatbots or models for open-ended text generation, using outputs as training targets, or working back from them to reverse engineer Anthropic's training methods. A narrow categoriser sits on the permitted side of that line; a general purpose staff chatbot is the case the restriction names.

rationales.A: Ownership of the outputs is real but it is not an unlimited licence. The restriction on training competing general purpose models sits alongside the ownership grant rather than being displaced by it.
rationales.C: Too restrictive. Outputs may be integrated into the customer's own applications and used to build specialised tools, so confining them to the originating workflow misstates the position.
rationales.D: Human review and keeping the work internal are good practice but they are not the condition the restriction turns on. What matters is the kind of model being trained, not who sees it.

items.objective: Identify appropriate and inappropriate use cases
items.stem: A defence contractor's compliance lead finds that one of the firm's analytical workflows runs into a restriction in Anthropic's Usage Policy. The firm's legal team asks whether it can apply to Anthropic for a carve-out from that restriction. What is the accurate answer?

options.text: Tailored restrictions are considered only for carefully vetted government entities, and a core set of prohibitions is never lifted.
Carve-outs are available to any customer on an Enterprise plan and are recorded as a variation in the commercial agreement.
Carve-outs are granted case by case to any customer that can evidence a lawful purpose and adequate safeguards against misuse.
No exceptions process exists at all; the Usage Policy applies identically to every customer, in every sector and every region, without variation.

items.explanation: Anthropic's published position is that the Usage Policy applies uniformly, with one narrow exception: it may tailor use restrictions for select government entities whose mission and legal authorities support responsible deployment, with foreign intelligence analysis conducted in accordance with applicable law given as the example. Even for those entities the core prohibitions are untouched, including disinformation campaigns, weapons development, censorship, domestic surveillance and malicious cyber operations, and the arrangement currently reaches only models classified at AI Safety Level 2 under the Responsible Scaling Policy. Eligibility turns on the entity's legal authorities, its safeguards against misuse and error, and independent democratic oversight. A commercial contractor cannot supply those, whatever its customer is.

rationales.B: Plan tier does not open the door. The exception is defined by the character of the entity and the oversight it sits under, not by what the customer has purchased or how large the contract is.
rationales.C: A lawful purpose and credible safeguards are part of the eligibility test, but they are not sufficient on their own. The process is confined to vetted government entities before those factors are ever weighed.
rationales.D: An overcorrection in the other direction. A narrow published exceptions process does exist; it is simply not open to commercial customers, which is a different thing from not existing.

The team proposes moving the work to the most capable model available and, on the strength of that, treating the housing officer's review of each letter as optional. What is the correct assessment?

The proposal is sound, because Opus is the most capable model and its accuracy removes the need for review.
The proposal is acceptable provided every letter carries a clear notice that AI helped produce it.

items.stem: A publisher's editorial director wants the firm's public archive kept out of AI model training, while its help pages stay retrievable when a reader asks Claude a question. She asks what Anthropic's crawlers make possible. Which TWO statements are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Anthropic runs separate crawlers for separate purposes, so blocking the training crawler does not stop pages being fetched for a user's request.
Opting out reaches back into the models Anthropic has already trained, so the archive is removed from those as well as from anything trained later.
Anthropic's crawlers honour standard robots.txt directives, and the rules have to be applied to each subdomain separately.
Blocking by IP address is the method Anthropic recommends, because it stops all of the company's crawler traffic in one step and needs no site changes.
Crawler control is a setting inside the organisation's Claude workspace rather than something published on the publisher's own web server.
One directive covers every Anthropic crawler at once, because all of them present the same user agent name when they request a page.

items.explanation: Anthropic documents three crawlers with different jobs: ClaudeBot collects web content for model training and development, Claude-User retrieves pages when a Claude user's request calls for them, and Claude-SearchBot indexes content to improve search results. Each has a different consequence when blocked, so an editorial policy that wants one outcome and not the other has to name the right agent rather than reaching for a blanket block. The crawlers respect standard robots.txt directives, and those rules apply per subdomain, so each subdomain to be restricted needs its own. Blocking by IP is expressly not recommended, because a bot blocked at the network layer may never read the robots.txt file that carries the instruction.

rationales.B: Opting out excludes future content from training datasets. It is a forward-looking control and not a mechanism for reaching into work already completed.
rationales.D: Anthropic advises against blocking by IP address for exactly this reason: a bot that cannot reach the site may not be able to read the robots.txt file that would have told it what to avoid.
rationales.E: This control lives on the publisher's own web server and is exercised by whoever administers the site. It is not a Claude workspace setting, and it applies to everyone's crawling, not only to the publisher's own staff.
rationales.F: The crawlers carry distinct user agent names precisely because they do distinct jobs, so a directive naming one of them leaves the other two entirely unaffected.
